title: Database
description: Storage engines, ACID semantics, concurrency control, horizontal scaling, and operational bottlenecks.

subtopics.title: SQL vs NoSQL
subtopics.subtitle: Choosing between relational ACID engines and distributed non-relational stores based on access patterns and scale.
keyTakeaways: SQL databases enforce strict schemas, foreign keys, and multi-row ACID transactions, making them ideal for complex relational domain models.
NoSQL stores trade arbitrary relational joins for horizontal partitionability and predictable sub-10ms latency at massive write scale.
The most common architectural mistake is adopting NoSQL for scalability when the domain model is inherently relational, forcing developers to build fragile client-side joins.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
SQL RELATIONAL MODEL VS NOSQL PARTITIONED MODEL
SQL (Normalized Relational Model with Joins):
[ Users Table ] <--- JOIN on user_id ---> [ Orders Table ] <--- JOIN on order_id ---> [ LineItems ]
(Guarantees referential integrity; difficult to partition across independent physical nodes)

NOSQL (Denormalized Partitioned Document / Wide-Column Model):
Partition Key: "user_102"
Value: { order_id: "ord_99", line_items: [ { sku: "A1", qty: 2 } ] }
(Everything fetched in a single O(1) primary key seek; scales horizontally across 100 nodes)

sections.heading: Storage Engines and Data Modeling Philosophies
sections.body: The division between SQL and NoSQL is primarily about access patterns and storage layout. Relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) store data in normalized tables to eliminate redundancy and maintain referential integrity. Queries assemble disparate records at runtime using relational JOINs. NoSQL systems (MongoDB, DynamoDB, Cassandra) optimize for access paths known in advance, grouping all data required by a single view into a single document or partition key to eliminate cross-node network joins.
bullets: Document Stores (MongoDB): Stores hierarchical JSON documents; flexible schemas; ideal for product catalogs and CMS content.
Wide-Column Stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB): Uses partitioned row keys with sorted clustering columns; optimized for high-volume append-only writes (chat logs, time-series metrics).
Key-Value Stores (Redis, DynamoDB): O(1) lookups by primary key; minimal query flexibility, but delivers single-digit millisecond latency at arbitrary scale.

codeSnippet.title: Data Access Comparison: Relational JOIN vs NoSQL Partitioned Document

sections.heading: Scaling Characteristics and Consistency Boundaries
sections.body: Relational engines scale vertically; scaling them horizontally requires complex application-level sharding that breaks multi-table foreign keys and joins. NoSQL systems were built from the ground up for horizontal distribution using consistent hashing rings, but sacrifice ad-hoc querying and multi-document ACID transactions.
bullets: Foreign Key Constraints: Relational databases guarantee that an order cannot point to a deleted user ID; NoSQL applications must handle orphaned references in application code.
Secondary Index Overhead: Global secondary indexes in NoSQL are maintained asynchronously, meaning secondary index lookups are eventually consistent.

The Polyglot Reality: Production systems rarely use just one. Modern platforms pair PostgreSQL for core transactional ledgers with DynamoDB for high-volume session data and Elasticsearch for free-text search.

tradeOffs.pros: Strict schema integrity; ad-hoc reporting via JOINs; battle-tested ACID transactions; mature ecosystem.
tradeOffs.cons: Horizontal write scaling requires manual sharding; schema migrations require locks on high-traffic tables.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Financial systems, ERPs, CRM platforms, e-commerce checkout, and relational domain graphs.

tradeOffs.pros: Predictable sub-10ms latency regardless of dataset size; linear horizontal scaling; automated partition rebalancing.
tradeOffs.cons: No cross-partition joins; querying by non-partition keys requires costly global secondary indexes or full table scans.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Real-time gaming state, IoT telemetry ingestion, shopping carts, chat history, and viral user sessions.

subtopics.interviewTip: Avoid claiming that NoSQL is 'better because it scales.' Senior engineers qualify their choice: 'We will use PostgreSQL because our domain requires multi-table relational integrity and ACID transactions. A single tuned instance handles 25k QPS, which satisfies our 5k QPS requirement. We will only introduce DynamoDB for unjoined event streams.'

subtopics.title: Database Bottlenecks
subtopics.subtitle: Diagnosing and resolving CPU saturation, Disk IOPS exhaustion, Lock Contention, N+1 queries, and MVCC bloat.
keyTakeaways: Database performance issues usually originate from one of four physical bottlenecks: CPU saturation, Disk IOPS exhaustion, Lock Contention, or Memory Buffer Thrashing.
The N+1 query antipattern saturates database connection pools and network bandwidth by issuing hundreds of individual queries inside application loops.
PostgreSQL MVCC table bloat and Transaction ID (XID) wraparound freeze occur when autovacuum cannot keep up with high write rates or long-running transactions.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
COMMON DATABASE PRODUCTION BOTTLENECKS
[ Application Pods ]
        |
        v (Connection Pool Exhaustion: 500 connections fighting for CPU)
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                  Database Primary Node                      |
| - CPU 100% (Missing Indexes, Sequential Scans, Hash Joins)  |
| - Disk IOPS 100% (High random writes, un-cached B-Tree seeks)|
| - Lock Contention (Hot row SELECT FOR UPDATE blocking Tx)   |
| - MVCC Bloat (Long-running query blocks VACUUM cleanup)     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

sections.heading: Query-Level Bottlenecks: N+1 Storms and Missing Indexes
sections.body: Most database performance crises start in application code rather than the database engine itself. ORM abstractions make it deceptively easy to introduce severe query amplification.
bullets: The N+1 Query Antipattern: Fetching 50 orders and then looping through each order to query its user (`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = order.user_id`) issues 51 sequential queries. Each query pays network RTT and connection overhead. Solved by eager loading (`JOIN` or `WHERE id IN (...)`).
Missing Composite Indexes: Queries sorting and filtering on multiple columns execute full sequential scans or temporary disk sorts when missing matching composite indexes.
Deep Offset Pagination: `OFFSET 100000` forces the database to scan and discard 100,000 index entries, burning CPU and disk IOPS.

codeSnippet.title: Eliminating the N+1 Antipattern via Batch IN Queries (DataLoader Pattern)

sections.heading: Storage Engine Bottlenecks: MVCC Bloat and Lock Contention
sections.body: Even with optimized queries, storage engines hit operational bottlenecks under heavy continuous write load.
bullets: Postgres MVCC Bloat: When rows update frequently, dead row versions accumulate. If a long-running transaction or forgotten analytics query stays open for hours, Postgres cannot vacuum dead rows newer than that transaction's snapshot. Tables balloon in size, degrading cache efficiency.

Transaction ID (XID) Wraparound: Postgres uses 32-bit transaction IDs (capping at ~2 billion transactions). If autovacuum cannot freeze old transaction IDs before reaching the limit, Postgres forcibly enters emergency read-only mode to prevent silent data corruption.

Hot-Row Lock Contention: If 500 concurrent threads execute `SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE`, they queue behind a single row lock. Throughput drops to the serial execution speed of a single core.

tradeOffs.pros: Fetches all related data in a single network round trip; database engine optimizes join execution plan.
tradeOffs.cons: Multiplies row volume over the wire if relations are one-to-many (cartesian product bloat).
tradeOffs.bestFor: One-to-one and simple one-to-many relationships.

tradeOffs.pros: Prevents cartesian product bloat; clean separation of queries; easy to cache individual entity queries.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires two network round trips; application must stitch relations in memory.
tradeOffs.bestFor: GraphQL resolvers and deep microservice domain models.

subtopics.interviewTip: When asked how to diagnose a slow database in production, outline a systematic debugging sequence: 'First, inspect database metrics to identify the physical bottleneck: CPU, Disk IOPS, Memory, or Connection Pool saturation. Second, query `pg_stat_statements` to find queries with the highest total execution time. Third, check `pg_stat_activity` for long-running transactions blocking autovacuum or holding exclusive row locks.'

subtopics.title: Connection Pooling
subtopics.subtitle: Managing database connections at scale with PgBouncer, ProxySQL, and transaction-level multiplexing.
keyTakeaways: Allocating too many database connections degrades throughput: CPU cores waste cycles on context-switching and lock contention rather than executing queries.
In PostgreSQL, each connection is an independent operating system process consuming 5-10 MB of memory; 1,000 idle connections waste ~10 GB of database RAM.
Transaction-level pooling via PgBouncer allows thousands of client applications to share a small pool of database connections, checking out a connection only while a transaction runs.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
TRANSACTION-LEVEL CONNECTION POOLING (PGBOUNCER)
[ 2,000 Application Client Connections ]
                 |
                 v (Client connections held idle between queries)
      [ PgBouncer Connection Proxy ]
                 |
                 v (Only 40 Active Physical Server Connections!)
      [ PostgreSQL Database Server ]
      (Zero process bloat; CPU cores execute queries at 100% efficiency)

sections.heading: Why Excessive Connections Degrade Performance
sections.body: A common operational mistake during traffic surges is increasing `max_connections` from 200 to 2,000. In PostgreSQL, each client connection spawns a dedicated OS process. Having 2,000 concurrent processes on a 16-core machine causes extreme kernel scheduling overhead, CPU cache thrashing, and memory exhaustion. The database spends more time context-switching between connections than executing SQL.
bullets: Process Memory Footprint: 2,000 connections allocate 10-20 GB of RAM solely for process state and connection buffers.
Lock Table Contention: Concurrent transactions share global memory structures for locking and snapshot visibility; higher connection counts inflate lock acquisition latency.
The Optimal Connection Sweet Spot: PostgreSQL performance peaks when active connection count is constrained to approximately `(2 * CPU cores) + disk channels`.

codeSnippet.title: PgBouncer Configuration for Transaction Pooling (pgbouncer.ini)
codeSnippet.code:
[databases]
production_db = host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=production_db

[pgbouncer]
listen_port = 6432
listen_addr = *
auth_type = scram-sha-256
# Transaction mode: connection returned to pool immediately on COMMIT/ROLLBACK
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 5000
default_pool_size = 40
reserve_pool_size = 10

sections.heading: Session vs Transaction vs Statement Pooling
sections.body: External connection proxies (PgBouncer for Postgres, ProxySQL for MySQL) operate under three distinct pooling modes.
bullets: Session Pooling: The client claims a physical database connection upon connect and holds it until disconnect. Provides basic connection reuse, but offers minimal multiplexing benefit during traffic spikes.

Transaction Pooling: The client claims a physical connection only for the duration of a transaction (`BEGIN ... COMMIT`). Between transactions, the client stays connected to PgBouncer while the underlying database connection serves other clients. Trade-off: session-level features (prepared statements, advisory locks, `SET search_path`) cannot be used safely.
Statement Pooling: The connection returns to the pool after each individual statement. Does not support multi-statement transactions.

tradeOffs.pros: Allows 10,000+ client connections to share 50 database connections; shields database from serverless scaling spikes.
tradeOffs.cons: Breaks session-level SQL features (temporary tables, named prepared statements without pgbouncer 1.21+ workarounds).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Serverless AWS Lambda architectures, microservice fleets, and high-concurrency web applications.

tradeOffs.pros: Full support for all session features, prepared statements, and advanced ORM capabilities; zero extra proxy hops.
tradeOffs.cons: Connection count scales linearly with application pod count; scaling up containers risks crashing the database.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Monolithic applications with fixed, predictable instance counts.

subtopics.interviewTip: When designing high-scale architectures with serverless functions (like AWS Lambda or Google Cloud Functions), always include an external connection pooler: 'Because serverless containers scale to thousands of instances in seconds, direct connections would crash the database. We will place PgBouncer or AWS RDS Proxy in front of the database to multiplex thousands of client connections into 50 physical connections.'

subtopics.title: Denormalization
subtopics.subtitle: Trading write complexity and storage redundancy for O(1) read performance using materialized views and event sync.
keyTakeaways: Normalization eliminates data redundancy and write anomalies; Denormalization duplicates data intentionally to eliminate costly runtime JOINs.
Denormalization improves read throughput from O(N) to O(1) by embedding child data or precomputing aggregations in parent rows.
The primary cost of denormalization is write amplification and data drift: every update must synchronize duplicated fields across multiple tables.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
NORMALIZED SCHEMA (Requires JOIN) VS DENORMALIZED (Single O(1) Read)
NORMALIZED (Requires 2 Table Lookups & JOIN on Every Read):
[ orders ] (id, user_id, total) ---> JOIN users ON orders.user_id = users.id ---> [ users ] (id, name, email)

DENORMALIZED (Direct Single-Table Read):
[ orders ] (id, user_id, user_name, user_email, total)
- Reading order details requires zero joins!
- Catch: When user updates email, an asynchronous worker must update all historical orders.

sections.heading: When and How to Denormalize Safely
sections.body: Normalization (3NF) is the gold standard for relational database design because each piece of information exists in exactly one place. This prevents anomalies: updating a user's name requires modifying a single row. However, as read traffic climbs to thousands of queries per second, executing 5-table JOINs on every page load saturates CPU and memory. Denormalization deliberately introduces redundancy to optimize read paths.
bullets: Precomputed Aggregations: Storing `comment_count` directly on the `posts` table instead of running `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM comments WHERE post_id = $1` on every feed load.
Attribute Duplication: Storing `author_name` and `author_avatar_url` directly inside the `comments` record to render comment feeds without joining the `users` table.

Immutable Historic Snapshots: Invoicing and order fulfillment must be denormalized by design. An order must freeze the product title, unit price, and shipping address at the exact moment of purchase, immune to subsequent product price updates.

codeSnippet.title: Asynchronous Denormalization Synchronization via Trigger / Event

sections.heading: Managing Write Amplification and Data Drift
sections.body: Denormalization shifts computational burden from the read path to the write path. A single update to an author's profile now triggers thousands of secondary updates across denormalized comment rows (Write Amplification).
bullets: Data Drift: If an asynchronous update worker crashes or drops an event, denormalized records permanently diverge from the primary source of truth.
Reconciliation Jobs: Run scheduled offline batch jobs (e.g., nightly Spark or SQL scripts) to detect and repair drift between source tables and denormalized views.
Materialized Views: Relational engines provide materialized views that precompute expensive queries and refresh periodically (`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY`).

tradeOffs.pros: Zero data redundancy; single-point-of-truth writes; no write amplification; immune to data drift anomalies.
tradeOffs.cons: Read queries require multi-table JOINs; read latency degrades as table sizes grow into millions of rows.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Internal transactional systems, ERPs, financial accounting, and write-heavy operational workflows.

tradeOffs.pros: O(1) read latency; zero database JOIN overhead; queries execute as simple single-table index seeks.
tradeOffs.cons: High write amplification; requires complex reconciliation pipelines to fix out-of-sync records.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-volume read-heavy social feeds, e-commerce product detail pages, and analytical dashboards.

subtopics.interviewTip: Distinguish between snapshot denormalization and mutable denormalization: 'In an e-commerce order, copying product title and unit price onto the order line item is mandatory snapshot denormalization, because historical receipts must never change when product catalog prices change. For mutable data like user avatars on comments, we trade write amplification for sub-5ms feed reads.'

subtopics.title: Indexing
subtopics.subtitle: Internal mechanics of B+ Trees, LSM-Trees, composite index prefix rules, selectivity, and covering indexes.
keyTakeaways: B+ Trees optimize for read latency and range scans via balanced leaf nodes on disk; LSM-Trees optimize for write throughput via sequential append-only flushes.

Composite indexes enforce the Leftmost Prefix Rule: an index on `(status, created_at)` accelerates queries filtering by `status` or `(status, created_at)`, but is useless for queries filtering by `created_at` alone.
Covering indexes include all queried columns in the index structure itself, allowing the database to execute Index-Only Scans without reading the heap table.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
B+ TREE STORAGE ENGINE VS LSM-TREE STORAGE ENGINE
B+ TREE (PostgreSQL / InnoDB): Balanced Tree on Disk
[ Root Node ] -> [ Internal Nodes ] -> [ Leaf Pages (Linked List) ]
- Reads: O(log N) fast page lookups; ideal for range scans
- Writes: In-place page updates; random disk I/O and page splits

LSM-TREE (Cassandra / RocksDB): Log-Structured Merge-Tree
[ In-Memory Memtable ] -> Flushed to -> [ Immutable SSTables on Disk ]
- Writes: Sequential disk appends (Fast!)
- Compaction: Background compaction merges SSTables, consuming disk IOPS

sections.heading: B+ Trees vs LSM-Trees Under the Hood
sections.body: Database indexing is dictated by underlying storage engine mechanics. Relational databases like Postgres and MySQL use B+ Trees. In a B+ Tree, data records or heap pointers are stored exclusively in sorted leaf nodes linked as a doubly linked list, with internal nodes holding navigation keys. This guarantees predictable `O(log N)` read and range-scan performance, but random updates force in-place disk modifications and page splits. LSM-Trees (used in Cassandra, RocksDB, and ScyllaDB) buffer writes in an in-memory memtable (Red-Black tree) and append flushed data to immutable sorted string tables (SSTables) on disk, achieving massive write throughput by converting random writes into sequential I/O.
bullets: B+ Tree Leaf Pointers: Leaf pages contain pointers to the actual table heap rows, unless the index is clustered (like MySQL InnoDB's primary key).

LSM Compaction Overhead: In LSM engines, reads must check the memtable, bloom filters, and multiple SSTables. Periodic background compaction merges SSTables to reclaim deleted tombstone space, consuming significant background disk IOPS.
Write Amplification: Every B+ Tree index added to a table increases the disk write amplification of every `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`.

codeSnippet.title: Composite Index and Covering Index Definition in PostgreSQL
codeSnippet.code:
-- 1. Composite Index: Supports (tenant_id), and (tenant_id, created_at)
-- Does NOT accelerate queries filtering by 'created_at' alone!
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_tenant_date 
ON orders (tenant_id, created_at DESC);

-- 2. Covering Index (Index-Only Scan):
-- Stores 'total_amount' directly in the leaf pages via INCLUDE clause.
-- The database reads the result directly from the index without touching table heap!
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_covering 
ON orders (tenant_id, status) 
INCLUDE (total_amount, user_id);

sections.heading: Selectivity, Cardinality, and the Leftmost Prefix Rule
sections.body: Creating an index does not guarantee the database query planner will use it. The planner evaluates column cardinality (the number of distinct values) and selectivity (the percentage of table rows matching the filter). If a query matches 30% of the table rows, the query planner will ignore the index and execute a full sequential scan because random page seeks across the index cost more than a linear sequential disk read.
bullets: High vs Low Cardinality: Primary keys, UUIDs, and email addresses have high cardinality (ideal for indexes); boolean flags (`is_active`) have low cardinality (indexes are ignored unless combined in composite keys).
Partial Indexes: In Postgres, index only the relevant subset (`CREATE INDEX ... WHERE status = 'PENDING'`). This keeps index size small and avoids indexing millions of archived records.
Index-Only Scans: When all columns referenced in the `SELECT`, `WHERE`, and `ORDER BY` clauses reside in the index itself, the database avoids reading the underlying table data pages completely.

tradeOffs.pros: Fast point reads and range scans; deterministic lookup times; immediate space reclamation on deletes.
tradeOffs.cons: Random write patterns reduce insertion throughput; index fragmentation requires periodic rebuilding.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Read-heavy relational workloads, transactional databases, and ordered range pagination.

tradeOffs.pros: Near line-rate sequential write performance; superior storage compression ratios on disk.
tradeOffs.cons: Slower read latency (read amplification); background compaction can cause sudden disk I/O and latency spikes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Write-heavy ingestion, IoT time-series telemetry, logging systems, and event ledgers.

subtopics.interviewTip: Demonstrate database mastery by explaining composite index ordering: 'When creating a composite index on `(status, created_at)`, equality filter columns must come first, followed by range filter columns. The database can seek to the equality value and then perform a sequential range scan along the index leaf pages.'

subtopics.title: Transactions
subtopics.subtitle: Guaranteeing Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability via Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and MVCC.
keyTakeaways: Database transactions bundle multiple operations into a single logical unit of work that either completely succeeds or leaves no trace.
Durability is achieved using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL): modifications are written sequentially to an append-only log on disk before modifying in-memory table pages.
Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) ensures readers never block writers and writers never block readers by maintaining multiple version snapshots of each row.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
WRITE-AHEAD LOGGING (WAL) & MVCC ROW SNAPSHOTS
[ Transaction Writes: Update Balance ]
                   |
                   v (Step 1: Synchronous Append)
[ Write-Ahead Log (WAL) on Disk ] -> fsync() confirms durability!
                   |
                   v (Step 2: Lazy Memory Write)
[ In-Memory Buffer Pool Pages ] (Marked "DIRTY", flushed to data files later)

MVCC ROW VERSIONING:
Row ID: 101 | Value: $100 | xmin: 450 | xmax: 510 (Old version, visible to Tx < 510)
Row ID: 101 | Value: $200 | xmin: 510 | xmax: 0   (New version, visible to Tx >= 510)

sections.heading: How ACID Operates Under the Hood: WAL and ARIES
sections.body: A database transaction is an abstraction that masks the messy physical realities of disk failures, operating system crashes, and concurrent memory access. To guarantee Durability and Atomicity without stalling on slow random disk writes, modern relational database engines implement Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) based on the ARIES recovery algorithm.
bullets: Write-Ahead Invariant: A database must never write a dirty data page from RAM to the permanent table files until the corresponding WAL log record is flushed to disk via `fsync()`.

Crash Recovery: On an unexpected crash and reboot, the engine scans the WAL. It executes a Redo phase to re-apply committed changes that were in memory, followed by an Undo phase to roll back uncommitted, partial transactions.
Group Commit: High-throughput databases batch WAL `fsync()` calls across multiple concurrent transactions, amortizing disk rotational or NVMe latency.

codeSnippet.title: Atomic Financial Ledger Transfer Transaction
codeSnippet.code:
-- Explicit ACID transaction block guaranteeing all-or-nothing execution
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

-- Deduct funds with balance constraint check
UPDATE accounts 
SET balance = balance - 250.00 
WHERE id = 'acc_alice' AND balance >= 250.00;

-- Credit target account
UPDATE accounts 
SET balance = balance + 250.00 
WHERE id = 'acc_bob';

-- Record immutable audit ledger entry
INSERT INTO ledger_entries (from_account, to_account, amount, created_at) 
VALUES ('acc_alice', 'acc_bob', 250.00, NOW());

COMMIT; -- Flushes WAL record to non-volatile disk

sections.heading: Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)
sections.body: Older database engines achieved isolation by locking rows or entire tables: readers placed shared locks that blocked writers, and writers placed exclusive locks that blocked readers. This destroyed concurrency. Modern engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle) solve this using MVCC. Instead of mutating rows in place, an update writes a new version of the row stamped with creation (`xmin`) and expiration (`xmax`) transaction IDs.
bullets: Non-Blocking Reads: A long-running analytics query reads snapshot versions created prior to its transaction start, completely unblocked by concurrent updates.

The Cost of MVCC (Table Bloat): Old row versions remain in table storage until removed. In PostgreSQL, the `VACUUM` process reclaims dead row space. Poorly tuned autovacuum causes catastrophic disk space bloat and performance degradation.

tradeOffs.pros: Guarantees zero data corruption and complete crash recovery; eliminates duplicate or partial state transitions.
tradeOffs.cons: Write throughput is bounded by disk `fsync` IOPS; distributed ACID across independent database nodes adds latency.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Financial transactions, billing ledgers, inventory reservation, and user account credentials.

tradeOffs.pros: Dramatically higher write throughput (10x+); decouples transaction commit acknowledgment from physical disk flush.
tradeOffs.cons: A server crash or power outage can lose the last 100-500ms of committed transactions.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Real-time gaming state, logging pipelines, session caches, and user activity counters.

subtopics.interviewTip: Explain why readers don't block writers in modern databases: 'Postgres and MySQL implement Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC). Each update writes a new version of the row with transaction timestamps, allowing readers to read a consistent snapshot without holding shared read locks.'

subtopics.title: Isolation Levels
subtopics.subtitle: Understanding concurrency anomalies (Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, Phantom Reads, Write Skew) and ANSI SQL guarantees.
keyTakeaways: Isolation levels represent an architectural compromise between transaction concurrency and the tolerance of data read anomalies.
Most production databases do NOT default to true Serializable isolation; PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed, while MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read (Snapshot Isolation).
Snapshot Isolation prevents non-repeatable reads and phantoms, but remains vulnerable to Write Skew unless guarded by explicit row locks or serializable concurrency.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
ISOLATION LEVELS & ANOMALY SPECTRUM
Isolation Level       | Dirty Reads | Non-Repeatable Reads | Phantoms | Write Skew
---------------------+-------------+----------------------+----------+------------
Read Uncommitted     | YES (Allowed)| YES                  | YES      | YES
Read Committed (PG)  | NO          | YES (Allowed)        | YES      | YES
Repeatable Read (MY) | NO          | NO                   | NO (MVCC)| YES (Vulnerable!)
Serializable         | NO          | NO                   | NO       | NO (Strict)

sections.heading: Concurrency Anomalies Explained
sections.body: When transactions execute concurrently, performance demands running them simultaneously rather than one by one. The ANSI SQL standard defines four isolation levels based on which anomalies they prevent.
bullets: Dirty Read: Transaction A reads data modified by Transaction B before Transaction B commits. If Transaction B rolls back, Transaction A acted on phantom data that never officially existed.
Non-Repeatable Read (Fuzzy Read): Transaction A reads a row, Transaction B updates that row and commits, and Transaction A re-reads the row to find different values.

Phantom Read: Transaction A queries a range of rows (`WHERE salary > 100k`), Transaction B inserts a new row matching that condition and commits, and Transaction A re-executes the query to find newly appeared rows.

Write Skew: Two transactions read overlapping data, find that business constraints are satisfied, and perform disjoint writes that collectively violate the constraint (e.g., two on-call doctors simultaneously unregistering because both saw two active doctors).

codeSnippet.title: Write Skew Anomaly Demonstration Under Repeatable Read

sections.heading: How Engines Implement Isolation Levels in Practice
sections.body: Understanding the difference between theory and implementation is critical. While ANSI SQL was written assuming lock-based concurrency (Two-Phase Locking), modern relational engines implement isolation via MVCC snapshots.
bullets: Read Committed (Postgres Default): Each individual query within a transaction takes a fresh MVCC snapshot. Eliminates dirty reads, but allows non-repeatable reads if another transaction commits between queries.
Repeatable Read (MySQL Default): The transaction takes a single MVCC snapshot at the moment of the first read. All subsequent reads see that identical snapshot, eliminating non-repeatable reads.

Serializable (SSI): PostgreSQL implements Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which detects overlapping read/write dependencies in memory without locking rows, aborting one of the conflicting transactions with a serialization failure (`40001`).

tradeOffs.pros: Maximum transaction throughput; minimal lock contention; zero serialization rollback failures.
tradeOffs.cons: Queries within the same transaction can observe changing row values; vulnerable to lost updates.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Standard CRUD applications, read-heavy dashboard APIs, and general web applications.

tradeOffs.pros: Mathematically guarantees zero concurrency anomalies, phantoms, or write skew; simplified application reasoning.
tradeOffs.cons: Higher abort rates under write contention; requires application-layer retry loops on serialization failures.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Complex financial auditing, multi-account ledger balancing, and legal contract state machines.

subtopics.interviewTip: Highlight Write Skew to demonstrate senior-level database knowledge: 'Snapshot Isolation (Repeatable Read) does not prevent Write Skew. If two concurrent transactions read overlapping state and update different rows to violate a shared business rule, both will commit. Preventing Write Skew requires either true Serializable isolation or explicit pessimistic row locking with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.'

subtopics.title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking
subtopics.subtitle: Preventing lost updates and double-booking in high-concurrency reservation and inventory systems.
keyTakeaways: Pessimistic locking acquires exclusive database locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), preventing concurrent transactions from touching the row until the transaction commits.
Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) uses a version column to detect conflicting updates at commit time, holding zero database locks during processing.
Use pessimistic locking when write contention is high (concert ticket drops); use optimistic locking when contention is low (editing user profiles).
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
OPTIMISTIC VS PESSIMISTIC LOCKING MECHANICS
PESSIMISTIC LOCKING (High Contention / Lock Row Immediately):
Client A: BEGIN -> SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (Lock Acquired) -------------> UPDATE -> COMMIT (Lock Released)
Client B: BEGIN -> SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (BLOCKED! Waits on lock) ---> UPDATE -> COMMIT

OPTIMISTIC CONCURRENCY CONTROL (Low Contention / Version Check):
Client A: Read row (v=1) -> Computes -> UPDATE ... WHERE id=1 AND v=1 (Succeeds! v becomes 2)
Client B: Read row (v=1) -> Computes -> UPDATE ... WHERE id=1 AND v=1 (0 rows updated! Conflict -> Retries)

sections.heading: Pessimistic Locking and Deadlock Prevention
sections.body: Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely. The moment a transaction reads a row it intends to modify, it acquires an exclusive lock via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. Any concurrent transaction attempting to read or modify that row is blocked by the database engine until the holding transaction commits or rolls back.
bullets: Eliminates Lost Updates: Guarantees that only one thread can inspect and mutate state at any given moment.

The Risk of Deadlocks: If Transaction 1 locks Account A then attempts to lock Account B, while Transaction 2 locks Account B and attempts to lock Account A, both block indefinitely. The database detects the deadlock and aborts one transaction.
Deadlock Prevention Rule: Always lock resources in a globally consistent order (e.g., sorting account IDs in ascending alphanumeric order before issuing locks).
Lock Contention Bottleneck: Hot rows (like a single inventory counter for a Taylor Swift concert) will queue thousands of transactions, exhausting connection pools.

codeSnippet.title: Pessimistic Locking with Consistent Lock Ordering to Prevent Deadlocks

sections.heading: Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) and Retry Loops
sections.body: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare. Transactions hold zero database locks during processing. Instead, each row includes a `version` integer or timestamp. When updating, the transaction verifies that the version in the database matches the version read initially. If another transaction updated the row in the interim, the version check fails, returning zero updated rows.
bullets: Zero Lock Contention: Read operations execute without holding locks, preserving maximum read and write concurrency.
Application Retry Loops: When an update returns 0 affected rows, the application catches the conflict, re-reads the fresh row version, and retries the business operation.
Thundering Herd Vulnerability: If 1,000 requests attempt to update the same row under OCC, 1 will succeed and 999 will fail and retry, flooding the database with wasted CPU work.

tradeOffs.pros: Guaranteed success for the lock holder; ideal when rollback cost is high or contention is severe; prevents wasted compute.
tradeOffs.cons: Risk of deadlocks; holds database locks across network round trips; exhausts connection pools under heavy load.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Flash sale inventory reservation, seat booking, banking transfers, and warehouse fulfillment.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero blocking locks; highest throughput when conflicts are rare; works seamlessly across disconnected user sessions.
tradeOffs.cons: Massive write contention causes high retry churn and wasted database CPU cycles.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Content management systems, user profile edits, document collaboration, and low-contention CRUD APIs.

subtopics.interviewTip: In high-concurrency ticket or inventory problems, state your locking strategy explicitly: 'Because write contention on seats is intense, optimistic locking would cause 99% of requests to fail and retry, overwhelming the database. We will use pessimistic locking with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and enforce strict alphabetical lock ordering across row IDs to eliminate deadlocks.'

subtopics.title: Replication
subtopics.subtitle: Single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless database replication topologies, WAL shipping, and failover mechanics.
keyTakeaways: Replication copies data across multiple physical machines to provide redundancy, failover protection, and read scaling.
Single-leader replication routes all writes through a primary node; asynchronous replication offers high write performance but risks data loss during ungraceful failover.
Multi-leader and leaderless topologies permit writes across multiple datacenters, but require conflict resolution mechanisms (LWW, vector clocks, or CRDTs).
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
REPLICATION TOPOLOGIES
1. SINGLE-LEADER (Primary-Replica via WAL Streaming):
   [ App Writes ] -> [ Primary Node ] === Async WAL Streaming ===> [ Read Replica 1 ]
                                                              ===> [ Read Replica 2 ]

2. LEADERLESS QUORUM (Dynamo / Cassandra):
   [ App Writes ] --- Concurrent writes to N replicas ---> [ Replica A (Ack) ]
                                                      ---> [ Replica B (Ack) ]
                                                      ---> [ Replica C (Slow/Down) ]
   (Write Quorum W=2 satisfied; background read-repair heals Replica C)

sections.heading: Physical vs Logical Replication and Log Shipping
sections.body: Replicating database state between nodes relies on streaming changes recorded in the transaction log. Relational engines support two distinct mechanisms for keeping replicas in sync.
bullets: Physical Streaming Replication: Streams raw byte-level disk changes from the Write-Ahead Log (WAL). Extremely fast and exact bit-for-bit duplicate; downside is that both primary and replica must run identical operating systems and database binary versions.

Logical Replication: Decodes the WAL into row-level change events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). Allows replicating a subset of tables, streaming data across different database versions for zero-downtime upgrades, and feeding external event systems like Kafka via Change Data Capture (CDC).

Synchronous vs Asynchronous: Synchronous replication guarantees that at least one replica has written the change to disk before acknowledging the client (RPO = 0), but client write latency includes network round trips to the replica.

codeSnippet.title: PostgreSQL Synchronous Standby Configuration (postgresql.conf)
codeSnippet.code:
# Enforce that writes are acknowledged only after at least 1 replica confirms disk commit
synchronous_commit = on
synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 1 (replica_az2, replica_az3)'
# If primary fails, zero committed transactions are lost (RPO = 0)!

sections.heading: Failover Hazards, Split-Brain, and Promotion Lag
sections.body: Promoting a standby replica to primary when the active leader fails is one of the most fraught operations in distributed database infrastructure.
bullets: Split-Brain Risk: If a primary becomes unreachable due to a localized network partition, a standby may self-promote to primary while the old primary continues accepting writes. This produces divergent data that requires manual reconciliation.
Fencing Tokens: Ensure that when a new primary is elected, the old primary is isolated (STONITH: Shoot The Other Node In The Head) or rejected via fencing generation tokens.
Replication Lag during Failover: In asynchronous replication, promoting a replica that lagged by 50ms drops all writes committed to the primary during that 50ms window.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero data loss during failover (RPO = 0); replica is guaranteed to hold identical state.
tradeOffs.cons: Every write pays cross-node or cross-AZ network latency; a single stalled replica can halt all primary writes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Core banking ledgers, critical authentication state, and high-compliance financial platforms.

tradeOffs.pros: Minimal write latency on the primary; primary continues operating even if all replicas drop offline.
tradeOffs.cons: Replication lag can cause stale reads; risk of losing un-replicated transactions if the primary dies ungracefully.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput read-heavy APIs, reporting databases, and cross-region disaster recovery standby nodes.

subtopics.interviewTip: When discussing database failover, explicitly address the trade-off between RPO and write latency: 'We will use semi-synchronous replication where the primary waits for acknowledgment from one local replica across Availability Zones before returning success. This guarantees zero data loss (RPO = 0) without paying cross-region latency.'

subtopics.title: Read Replicas
subtopics.subtitle: Scaling read-heavy workloads while solving replication lag anomalies: Read-Your-Writes, Monotonic Reads, and LSN pinning.
keyTakeaways: Read replicas scale read-heavy applications (10:1 to 100:1 read-to-write ratios) by offloading queries from the primary database instance.
Asynchronous replication lag causes read-after-write anomalies: a user updates their profile, refreshes the page, and observes their old data.
Mitigate replication lag anomalies using Read-Your-Own-Writes routing: pin user reads to the primary database for 5-10 seconds following a write.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
READ REPLICA TRAFFIC ROUTING WITH WRITE PINNING
[ Client ] ---> [ API Server ]
                     |
       +-------------+-------------+
       | Writes & Pinned Reads     | Normal Reads
       v                           v
[ Primary Database ] === Async ===> [ Read Replica Pool ]
(Handles all INSERT/UPDATEs)        (Handles 90% of read traffic)
(Handles reads for 10s post-write)

sections.heading: Consistency Anomalies Caused by Replication Lag
sections.body: Deploying read replicas is the standard pattern for scaling relational databases. However, because replication between primary and replicas is almost always asynchronous to keep write latency low, replicas lag behind the primary by milliseconds to seconds under load. This lag introduces severe client anomalies.
bullets: Read-Your-Writes Anomaly: A user changes their email address and clicks Save. The write commits to the primary. The browser immediately requests the updated profile, which routes to a read replica lagging by 500ms. The user sees their old email and assumes the save failed.

Monotonic Read Inversion: A user refreshes a comment thread twice. The first read hits a caught-up replica and shows 10 comments. The second read hits a lagging replica and shows 8 comments. The user observes time travel.
Replica Lag Spikes: Long-running analytical queries, batch migrations, or network saturation on replicas can inflate lag from 10ms to tens of seconds.

codeSnippet.title: Session-Pinned Read-Your-Writes Router Middleware

sections.heading: Architectural Patterns for Replica Routing
sections.body: Application architectures employ three common patterns to route traffic across primary and replica pools cleanly.
bullets: Connection-Level Splitting: Application code or ORMs maintain two distinct connection pools: `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` routes to replicas, while standard transactions route to primary.
Database Proxy Routing: Reverse proxies like ProxySQL or AWS RDS Proxy inspect incoming SQL statements; queries starting with `SELECT` route to replicas, while `INSERT/UPDATE` route to the primary.

LSN Watermarking: The primary returns its Log Sequence Number (LSN) upon commit. The client passes this token on subsequent reads; replicas serve the request only if their local replay LSN matches or exceeds the client's token.

tradeOffs.pros: Completely eliminates user confusion after mutations; simple to implement via Redis session keys.
tradeOffs.cons: Momentarily routes read traffic for active users to the primary, increasing primary load.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Interactive consumer web apps, social profile updates, and settings dashboards.

tradeOffs.pros: Guarantees mathematically exact consistency without over-routing traffic to the primary.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires database engine support for Global Transaction IDs (GTID) and client token propagation.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Financial accounting portals, order status tracking, and enterprise SaaS.

subtopics.interviewTip: Whenever proposing read replicas in a design interview, anticipate the interviewer's next question: 'Because replication is asynchronous, we must prevent read-your-writes anomalies. We will store a timestamp in Redis whenever a user updates data and route that specific user's reads to the primary for the next 5 seconds, ensuring they immediately see their changes.'

subtopics.title: Sharding
subtopics.subtitle: Horizontal data partitioning across independent database nodes: Shard Keys, Routing, Resharding, and Cross-Shard Joins.
keyTakeaways: Sharding splits a massive database into independent, isolated physical instances (shards), each holding a subset of rows.
Shard key selection is a permanent architectural commitment: choosing a poor shard key causes uneven data distribution and hotspotting.
Sharding eliminates single-node hardware limits, but sacrifices cross-shard joins, distributed ACID transactions, and foreign key integrity.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
DATABASE SHARDING TOPOLOGY & QUERY ROUTER
[ Client Query: WHERE tenant_id = 't_99' ]
                    |
                    v
         [ Routing Proxy / Vitess ]
         (Computes hash(t_99) % 3 = Shard 1)
                    |
      +-------------+-------------+
      |                           |
      v                           v
[ Shard 0 (Postgres) ]      [ Shard 1 (Postgres) ]      [ Shard 2 (Postgres) ]
(Tenants 0-333)             (Tenants 334-666)           (Tenants 667-999)

sections.heading: Shard Key Selection and Routing Mechanics
sections.body: Sharding should be your last resort when scaling a database—only when write IOPS or storage volume exceeds the limits of the largest available vertical hardware. Once you shard, selecting the shard key (partition key) dictates how traffic and storage distribute across the cluster.
bullets: Hash-Based Sharding: Computes `hash(shard_key) % num_shards`. Distributes rows uniformly across shards, but makes range queries (`WHERE created_at BETWEEN X AND Y`) scatter-gather across every single shard.

Range-Based Sharding: Partitions data by contiguous ranges (e.g., User IDs 1-1000 on Shard A, 1001-2000 on Shard B). Supports efficient range scans, but creates extreme hot shards if rows are inserted with auto-incrementing timestamps.
Directory-Based Sharding: Uses an external lookup table or consistent hashing ring to map entity IDs to shard locations, enabling flexible data migrations at the cost of an extra lookup hop.

codeSnippet.title: Consistent Hash Shard Router with Virtual Nodes

sections.heading: Solving Cross-Shard Queries and Re-Sharding
sections.body: The operational cost of sharding emerges when business logic requires querying data stored across multiple physical shards.
bullets: Scatter-Gather Queries: If a query cannot filter by the shard key (e.g., `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_email = 'alice@example.com'` on an `order_id`-sharded database), the router must dispatch queries to all shards in parallel and merge results in memory.

Cross-Shard Joins: Traditional relational JOINs across shards are impossible. Applications must either denormalize data into the same shard, or query each shard independently and join in application memory.

Re-Sharding Complexity: When growing from 4 shards to 8 shards, modulo hashing (`hash % 4` to `hash % 8`) remaps ~75% of all keys. Using virtual bucket mapping (e.g., 1,024 fixed virtual buckets distributed across physical shards) ensures adding nodes only moves `1/N` keys.

tradeOffs.pros: Full ACID transactions; native relational JOINs; zero routing infrastructure; simple backups.
tradeOffs.cons: Hard physical limits on CPU, memory, and write IOPS; high cost at top cloud instance tiers.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Most systems handling under 20,000 writes/sec and under 5 TB of relational data.

tradeOffs.pros: Virtually unlimited storage and write throughput capacity; bounds the blast radius of single-node hardware failures.
tradeOffs.cons: Eliminates cross-shard ACID transactions; schema migrations require coordinating across dozens of nodes; complex resharding.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Hyperscale multi-tenant SaaS, global social networks, and payment engines processing 50k+ writes/sec.

subtopics.interviewTip: In system design interviews, never jump straight to sharding without justifying it with numbers: 'A single AWS RDS Postgres instance can handle 20,000 writes per second. Because our peak write volume is 60,000 writes/sec, we are forced to shard. We will shard by `tenant_id` to ensure that 99% of queries remain single-shard operations.'

subtopics.title: Partitioning
subtopics.subtitle: Single-node table partitioning (Range, List, Hash), Vertical Partitioning, and Partition Pruning for massive tables.
keyTakeaways: Table partitioning splits a large table into smaller physical sub-tables on a single database node while presenting a single unified table view to applications.
Partition Pruning allows the query planner to inspect `WHERE` clauses and read only the matching partition, completely skipping gigabytes of unneeded data.
Dropping an expired month partition via `DROP TABLE` is an instant O(1) operation that generates zero WAL overhead, unlike `DELETE` which causes severe table bloat.
subtopics.architectureDiagram:
SINGLE-NODE RANGE PARTITIONING & PRUNING
Query: SELECT * FROM audit_logs WHERE created_at = '2026-10-03';

[ Unified Parent Table: audit_logs ]
                 |
        Query Planner Pruning
                 |
  +--------------+--------------+
  |                             |
  v (Pruned / Skipped)          v (Scanned Directly)
[ audit_logs_2026_09 ]        [ audit_logs_2026_10 ]
(Not touched by disk I/O!)    (Sub-millisecond index seek)

sections.heading: Horizontal Partitioning: Range, List, and Hash
sections.body: Unlike sharding (which distributes data across independent network servers), single-node table partitioning divides a massive table into smaller physical backing tables within the same database engine. When a table grows to hundreds of millions of rows, its B-Tree indexes exceed available RAM, turning every query into a slow random disk seek. Partitioning keeps individual sub-table indexes small enough to fit in the database buffer pool cache.
bullets: Range Partitioning: Partitions by date or numeric range (e.g., one partition per calendar month). Ideal for time-series data, transaction logs, and audit trails.
List Partitioning: Partitions by explicit discrete values (e.g., `country_code IN ('US', 'CA')`). Best for regulatory data residency compliance on a single server.
Hash Partitioning: Partitions by a modulus hash of a key to evenly distribute rows across a fixed number of sub-tables.

Partition Pruning: The database query optimizer detects partition constraints in queries (`WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-01'`) and scans only the October partition, ignoring all other historical partitions.

codeSnippet.title: PostgreSQL Declarative Range Partitioning by Month

sections.heading: Vertical Partitioning: Row Splitting and TOAST
sections.body: Vertical partitioning splits a wide table with dozens of columns into separate tables sharing the same primary key, separating frequently accessed hot columns from rarely accessed wide text columns.
bullets: Column Isolation: Moving wide columns (`user_bio TEXT`, `resume_pdf BLOB`) to a separate table (`user_profiles_extended`) allows the primary `users` table to pack ten times more rows per 8 KB database page, dramatically increasing buffer pool cache efficiency.
TOAST in PostgreSQL: Postgres automatically vertical-partitions large fields out-of-line into TOAST (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique) tables when row size exceeds 2 KB.

tradeOffs.pros: O(1) data lifecycle pruning via `DROP TABLE`; queries benefit from partition pruning; indexes fit into memory.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires automated cron jobs to provision upcoming month partitions; queries without partition keys must scan all sub-tables.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Time-series logging, financial audit records, and analytical event tables.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero partition management overhead; global unique constraints enforced natively by database engine.
tradeOffs.cons: B-Tree indexes eventually exceed RAM; data retention deletes (`DELETE FROM ... WHERE created_at < ...`) saturate WAL and cause table bloat.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Small to medium tables (<10 million rows) with uniform access patterns.

subtopics.interviewTip: When discussing historical data retention (e.g., storing 5 years of logs but purging data older than 90 days), recommend Range Partitioning: 'Instead of running an expensive DELETE query that causes massive WAL write spikes and table bloat, we range-partition audit logs by month. Purging data older than 90 days is a sub-millisecond `DROP TABLE` operation that instantly reclaims disk space.'
